title: Hamilton councillor says he's been 'silenced' by police board as conduct probe hits one-year mark
subtitle: Cameron Kroetsch believes complaints about previous members have been handled differently
article: A Hamilton councillor says a conduct investigation that's sidelined him from police board meetings for more than a year is "personally motivated."

Coun. Cameron Kroetsch was suspended from Hamilton's police board in March 2024 when the Ontario Civilian Police Commission (OCPC) notified him of a probe into his conduct following a complaint from a former board chair.

In a public letter Monday, the downtown councillor railed against the board and provincial watchdog, writing the dragged-out investigation has "effectively silenced" one of the board's most vocal voices "for a full year."

"As time has worn on, it's become even clearer to me that the actions the original board took in filing this complaint were procedurally unfair, an abuse of process, biased and personally motivated," Kroetsch wrote in the letter.
What's known about the year-long suspension is limited to letters Kroetsch has published online.
The OCPC has for months refused to acknowledge a probe even exists, saying in a statement Monday it can't comment "on the substance or circumstances of ongoing investigations."
The commission is mandated to oversee police disciplinary issues and procedures that govern police services. Among other responsibilities, it probes alleged conduct violations by board members.

Kroetsch was asked to step aside for the OCPC investigation on March 8, 2024, about two months after the board filed a pair of conduct complaints against him, according to a letter he published at the time. The complaints related to a motion he introduced to direct the use of police and library budget surpluses, as well as social media posts that criticized the board's budget process.
In Monday's letter, Kroetsch said the OCPC interviewed him about the alleged conduct breaches for the first time last September.
"(This) was the only time I've spoken directly with the anyone from the OCPC over the last year," he wrote.

Instead, as the probe stalled, Kroetsch claims the OCPC accepted a request from the board to add more allegations to its list of conduct violations, including that the councillor made public comments about last year's budget and attended a rally in support of a man recently shot dead by Hamilton police.
Over a call, Kroetsch said he learned about the new allegations from the OCPC, not the board.

That's in violation of the latter's policy for conduct complaints, which states the board must send accused members complaints and allow them to respond in writing. The board reviews the response before it decides to either dismiss the complaint, take action or forward it to the OCPC, according to the policy.
"None of that happened here," Kroetsch said, noting he couldn't respond to the new complaints because the OCPC had already accepted the board's request to investigate them.

"The public should know about this because this isn't how accountability and transparency work. Boards, especially boards managing a quarter-billion-dollar budget, should have more transparency and accountability in how they address complaints."
The OCPC didn't respond to questions about the new complaints.
It's also unclear when the board allegedly decided to forward more complaints to the watchdog.

Don Robertson, who was acclaimed as board chair in January, said Kroetsch's suspension came "long before my time." He said he hasn't spoken with the OCPC about any investigation, isn't aware of new allegations and has never met the downtown councillor.
Coun. Esther Pauls, a longtime board member, wouldn't say when or if the board sent new allegations to the OCPC.

But she alleged over a call "people are complaining" about Kroetsch, pointing specifically to tweets about the police budget and attending a vigil for Erixon Kabera in the city hall forecourt Nov. 14. Kabera, 43, was fatally shot after an "interaction" with two Hamilton officers in his condo building, according to the Special Investigations Unit.
"We're supposed to instil confidence in our police service, not question them," Pauls said.

She added of the investigation still not finished after more than a year: "I know he's complaining it's taking too long, but it's because he keeps on tweeting things and saying things that (disparage) the police."
Anjali Menezes, a civilian board member, noted she was also at the vigil for Kabera. She wouldn't discuss the OCPC investigation, but said there were no complaints filed related to her attendance.
"I fully support member Kroetsch and look forward to his complaint being dismissed," she said in a call.

Mayor Andrea Horwath, another board member, said she sympathizes with Kroetsch's frustrations and that his time in limbo "is impacting the board." She added of the additional complaints cited by Kroetsch: "That's not something that I was involved in."
Kroetsch's suspension from the board is the longest since at least 2013, when ex-councillor Terry Whitehead was sidelined for four months amid an OCPC probe.
Kroetsch argues the OCPC has handled his case differently than others.
Consider former board chair Lloyd Ferguson, who in 2017 was investigated for saying a Hamilton police officer - accused of "carding" then-councillor Matthew Green - was charged "for doing his job."

Ferguson was notified about the conduct investigation and required to step away from the board on Dec. 18, 2017, a week before Christmas and a period of the year when the board doesn't meet. He met with commission investigators a day later, Dec. 19, and expressed regret for his conduct. By Jan. 8, the OCPC issued its decision and handed the councillor a retroactive three-week suspension - meaning he didn't miss a board meeting.

"I acknowledge that every complaint is different," Kroetsch said in the letter, "but I'm concerned this appears to be an attempt to keep me off the board for a prolonged period of time to prevent me from providing oversight on behalf of the residents of Hamilton."
This story was updated March 11 to correct that the police budget is close to a quarter-billion dollars.
